I could only read three commentaries in depth for Isaiah 62: David Guzik's Enduring Word, Matthew Henry (from search excerpts, since the full page didn't load properly), and the BibleHub chapter page. I also found one short excerpt from Gray's Concise Commentary. I hit my search and fetch limits before reaching Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Precept Austin, the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, or any Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal source. So parts 2 and 3 are thin, and I haven't put denominational labels on these writers because the pages don't state them.

**Main sources**
- Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-62/
- Matthew Henry: https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_062.cfm

## Verse-by-verse notes

**Whole chapter: how to read "Zion"**
- **Guzik:** Zion is a real place, but it also stands for Israel and, more broadly, a representation of all God's people. (Enduring Word)
- **Matthew Henry:** The promises apply to the Jews after they came back from exile, and for the Christian church when it shall be set up in the world. (Henry)
- **Gray's (a future-Israel reading):** Gray places the chapter at the opening of the Millennial age. In his view Israel is back in its land, mostly not yet believing in Christ and worshiping in a rebuilt temple. (Gray's)
- This is the biggest interpretive split I found: Henry and Guzik apply the chapter to the church, while Gray reads it as a future end-times event for national Israel.
- **BibleHub:** Chapter 61 introduced the Herald anointed by the Spirit, and chapter 62 shows how his message reshapes Zion. It does this by giving her a new identity, constant prayer covering, and world-wide recognition. (BibleHub)

**v. 1**
- **Who is speaking?**
  - Guzik takes the speaker to be the LORD himself, who will not rest until Jerusalem shines with righteousness. (Enduring Word)
  - Henry takes it to be the prophet, who resolves to keep preaching and praying. He sees him as a type of Christ, who never tired in his work as a prophet. (Henry)
  - So this verse has two different readings of the speaker.
- **Setting (Guzik):** Isaiah wrote while Jerusalem still stood but was spiritually corrupt. He looks ahead to the city destroyed by Babylon and comforts its discouraged people. (Enduring Word)
- **Ministers (Henry):** He draws a lesson for pastors: The business of ministers is to speak from God to his people and to God for his people. (Henry)
- **Why the prophet keeps on (Henry):** Isaiah would not live to see the return from Babylon or the coming of the gospel. Henry says his words keep speaking anyway, and in every age a faithful remnant keeps praying for these things. (Henry)
- **Cross-reference (BibleHub):** Matthew 5:14–16, the light of righteousness shining for the nations. (BibleHub)

**v. 2**
- **The nations (Guzik):** When God lifts up Zion, the nations see it and come to trust the LORD themselves, kings included. (Enduring Word)
- **The new name (Guzik):** The LORD who transforms the city also gives it its new name. Guzik extends this to Christians, who will receive new names in heaven (Revelation 2:17; 3:12). (Enduring Word)
- **The new name (BibleHub):** In Scripture a new name marks a new role, as with Abram becoming Abraham and Simon becoming Peter. Here it seals Zion's change from shame to delight. (BibleHub)

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** We usually think of *receiving* a crown. Here God's people *are* the crown in God's hand. He links this to Ephesians 1:18, which speaks of God's inheritance in his people, not just theirs in him. (Enduring Word)
- **Henry:** The crown is in God's *hand*, not on his head (as adding any real honour or power to him. (Henry)

**v. 4**
- **The old names (Henry):** "Forsaken" and "Desolate" describe the exile, when Zion was like a woman reproachfully divorced or left a disconsolate widow. (Henry)
- **The new names (Guzik):** Hephzibah means "My delight is in her" and Beulah means "Married." They speak of God's delight and his unbroken presence. Guzik quotes Motyer, who links this to the marriage of the Lamb in Revelation 19:7. (Enduring Word)
- **Hephzibah as a real name (Henry and BibleHub):**
  - Henry notes it was the name of Hezekiah's queen, Manasseh's mother (2 Kings 21:1). (Henry)
  - BibleHub suggests Isaiah may be reclaiming a royal memory to promise a royal future. (BibleHub)
- **Other links (BibleHub):** Revelation 21:2, the bride adorned for her husband, and Hosea 2:16–20, God as husband. (BibleHub)

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** God's love here is not just duty; he will *rejoice over* his people. Guzik links this to Zephaniah 3:17 and Ephesians 3:18–19. (Enduring Word)
- None of the pages I read discussed the unusual phrase "your sons will marry you."

**vv. 6–7: the watchmen**
- **Guzik:** The watchmen are not critics; they are prayer warriors, who give God no rest. (Enduring Word)
- **Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik):** God invites us to be persistent with him: to press him, wrestle with him, and lay hold of his strength. (Enduring Word)
- **Bultema (quoted by Guzik):** He applies the passage specifically to prayer for Israel's deliverance. (Enduring Word)
- **Henry:** He reads the watchmen as ministers who stand guard over the church, and links "give him no rest" to Luke 11:5–8. (Henry) He adds that when God plans mercy for a people, he first brings them to their duty and pours out a spirit of prayer upon them. (Henry)
- So again there are two emphases: prayer for Israel (Bultema) versus ministers and prayer for the church (Henry).
- **BibleHub:** The watchmen echo the old Near Eastern custom of temple singers chanting day and night. (BibleHub)

**vv. 8–9**
- **Guzik:** Jerusalem will no longer be plundered; those who grow the harvest will eat it and praise the LORD. (Enduring Word)
- **Henry:** Losing the crops was a double blow, because the people went hungry while their enemies grew stronger. He draws the lesson that we should gather God's gifts with care and enjoy them gladly. (Henry)
- **BibleHub:** God swears by his right hand to show the promise is certain. (BibleHub)

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** The road must be built and cleared for the great pilgrimage to Jerusalem promised earlier in Isaiah. The banner marks the way, so that people are not only *able* to come but *drawn* to come. (Enduring Word)
- **BibleHub:** It applies the verse to removing obstacles so neighbors meet their Savior. (BibleHub)
- **Henry:** He reads verses 10–12 as the return from Babylon and, as a picture of that, the redemption won by Christ. (Henry)

**v. 11**
- **Guzik:** The Savior came to Zion, but not only to Zion, since the news goes "to the end of the world." He says Revelation 22:12 quotes this verse, and links the "reward" to 1 Corinthians 3:8–14: believers judged by their work. (Enduring Word)
- **Henry:** A message announced to the whole world must have a reference to the gospel of Christ. (Henry)
- **BibleHub:** Revelation 22:12 puts Jesus' voice behind this promise, which confirms Isaiah 62 as a hope about the Messiah. (BibleHub)

**v. 12**
- **Henry:**
  - "Holy People" means Christians are "saints" (1 Corinthians 1:2). He adds that None are to be called the redeemed of the Lord but those that are the holy people. (Henry)
  - "Sought Out": holiness gives a place an honour that makes others seek it. (Henry)
- **Guzik:** Jerusalem, so often forsaken, will be known by all as valued and chosen by God. (Enduring Word)
